title: Characterizing symptom prominence in persistent postconcussion symptoms using random ensembles of person-specific networks.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This article aimed to evaluate the feasibility of an idiographic, network-based symptom prominence classification approach using short-term ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data in individuals with persistent postconcussion symptoms and to examine its associations with clinical and demographic characteristics.
METHOD: Forty adults with clinician-diagnosed concussion completed baseline neuropsychological assessment and 20 days of EMA (21 symptoms, five assessments daily). Random symptom ensembles of graphical vector autoregressive models were used to estimate individualized symptom networks.
RESULTS: Thirty-eight participants (= 42.5; 23 female) provided sufficient EMA data (mean adherence = 79.1%). Person-specific symptom ensembles met classification criteria for classification in 31 of the 38 participants (81.6%). Symptom prominence classifications (emotional, cognitive, somatic) were derived using centrality metrics, with moderate agreement across operationalizations (κ = 0.55; 71.0%). Somatic and cognitive classifications were the most common. Greater psychological distress was associated with higher odds of emotional relative to cognitive classification across both operationalizations, whereas higher overall symptom burden showed the opposite pattern. Sex was not reliably estimable: All participants with an emotional-dominant classification under the highest mean operationalization were female, producing complete separation.
CONCLUSIONS: Idiographic network modeling from short-term EMA data is feasible and may support characterization of symptom network organization in persistent postconcussion symptoms. Findings are preliminary and exploratory given the modest sample size and lack of external validation. Further research is needed to determine the validity, stability, and clinical utility of these classifications. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).
